docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Welcome to my Documentation Hub. This is where all my documentation regarding my current Raspberry Pi and Proxmox server Projects are hosted.

This allows me to share the work I have done, and all the steps and configuration. This is hosted via GitHub Pages, with the site pages created using MKDocs (with Material).

Any configuration files that are shareable, will be held on my GitHub repo, named Pi-Homelab. You can get to this using the link found at the top-right corner of the site.

To get started, click on any of the left-side tabs.

docs.title: 1. Initial Connection Setup
docs.text: For displaying and presenting my configs, documentation, and GitHub Pages, setting up GitHub on the Raspberry Pi is key. This is how I am currently hosting my documentation, as well as my configuration on the repo.

docs.title: Deployment of the GitHub Package
docs.text:
Ensure first that github is installed on the device:

sudo apt install git -y

We can then run through the following commands, to set our global username and email address. Enter your personal username and email address in place of "user" and "user@mail.com":

git config --global user.name "user"
git config --global user.email "user@mail.com"

To view what has been set:

git config --list

docs.title: SSH Key
docs.text:
To avoid entering your username and password every time you interact with remote repositories, we can setup an SSH key, so that this automatically authenticates with the device (Raspberry Pi).

To do this, we can generate the key using the following command:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "user@mail.com"
- When prompted, you can press enter for the default path - It will also prompt you for a passphrase. Press enter to skip if not needed

SSH Key under /home/user/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Pass Phrase is: Enter Pass Phrase

We can then copy the SSH key to our clipboard, so we can add it to github. We can use the following command to export and copy the file:

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

We can then use this string for our new SSH key on Github:

  1. Login to Github
  2. Click on your Profile Picture and select Settings
  3. Click on the SSH and GPG keys tab
  4. Click New SSH key
  5. Enter the name of the key, which will be Raspberry Pi 4 Git Key
  6. Paste the key string, including 'ssh-ed' and your username/email at the end
  7. Press Add SSH Key

We can test the connection via the following command:

ssh -T git@github.com

It will appear with a warning to say it can't be established, but press yes to trust the key. It will then ask for your pass phrase, and confirm connection.

docs.title: 1. Installation & Setup
docs.text: Vaultwarden is used to locally host your own Bitwarden Password Manager. This will be installed via a Docker Compose installation.

docs.title: Docker Compose Creation
docs.text:
Firstly, we can create out .yaml compose file under directory ~/pihomelab/docker-compose The following is to be entered on the file:

sudo nano vaultwarden-compose.yaml

services:
  vaultwarden:
    image: vaultwarden/server:latest
    container_name: vaultwarden
    restart: unless-stopped
    dns:
      - ${UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP} # To ensure Vaultwarden uses Unbound (Docker IP)
      - ${PI_IP} # Fallback to Pi IP as DNS
    networks:
      swarm_network:
    environment:
      DOMAIN: ${DOMAIN}  # enter your domain
      SIGNUPS_ALLOWED: "false"                  # disable after creating your first account
      ADMIN_TOKEN: ${ARGON2_HASH}
    volumes:
      - ${VAULTWARDEN_VOLUME}:/data

networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true
    driver: overlay

networks: - Connected to our docker network, allowing for DNS communication, and working alongside Nginx.

docs.title: Admin Token
docs.text:
For 'ADMIN_TOKEN', as we're hosting this file on Github, I have created a .env file to keep this on, with ${ARGON2_HASH} being called from it.

Under the same directory, I have ran sudo nano .env, and added the following inside:

ARGON2_HASH='INSERT_HASH_HERE'
DOMAIN=vault.user.local

docs.title: Generating encrypted ARGON2 Hash
docs.text:
To obtain and securely generate the ARGON2 hash code, we can generate a PHC code using Bitwarden defaults. There are a few methods of doing this, but the simplest is creating a temporary docker container:

docker run --rm -it vaultwarden/server:latest /vaultwarden hash

This will prompt for a password upon running the command; Enter a secure password (this will be your admin password). The output will then generate something similar to this:

$argon2id$v=14$n=233421,t=3,p=8$kK31413FFEsfCxSDdddwCF9LYXqrP312WERWgh2asdaff3E8ozeV+fsf324fgg5aJrRax4324fDVVDns8M

Paste what is generated into the env file, but making sure the single quotes are used at the start and end of the token.

Once the compose file is setup and ready, and setting the port number to be used, we can run the installation:

sudo docker compose -f vaultwarden-compose.yaml up -d

docs.title: HTTPS Setup
docs.text:
As Vaultwarden requires HTTPS to function, and allow you onto the vault, we have to make sure this is setup on our reverse proxy, Nginx.

Please refer to [Vaultwarden Server Block], and HTTPS steps breakdown via [4. HTTPS Configuration].

docs.title: Initial Setup
docs.text:
Once HTTPS is setup, we can proceed on creating our login. On the browser, enter address vault.user.local.

On loading up the webpage, you will be presented with the Vaultwarden login interface. As this is a selfhosted Bitwarden vault, you won't be able to use an existing Bitwarden account. Therefore, we will need to create a new login.

Click Create Account, and setup your login.

![[Pasted image 20260818212702.png|406]]

docs.title: Exporting and Importing Passwords
docs.text: Once in, we can import our passwords. If you have password stored on a normal Bitwarden account, you can export these via the portal to a .json file.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Tools > Export
  2. Select file format .json
  3. Press Export, and select the area on your machine you'd like to store the file on

docs.title: Import
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Tools > Import
  2. Under Destination, select My vault, and leave the folder blank
  3. Under Data, select file format Bitwarden (json), and click Choose file
  4. Select the .json file on your machine, and press Import

When imported, all passwords should successfully transfer onto the account.

docs.title: Updating Vaulwarden
docs.text:
As for all docker containers, please ensure that the containers are updated with the latest image!!

We can tell if it is out-of-date, due to the browser extensions, mobile app, and desktop app of Bitwarden are not successfully pulling the passwords, and can also be checked via https://vault.user.local/admin/diagnostics.

Simply run the command below to pull the latest image, and then stop the container, delete the container, and reinstall it again from the compose.yaml file:

docker pull vaultwarden/server:latest

docs.title: 1. Installation for MkDocs
docs.text:
MKDocs is used as a site generator, which I will be using to host my homelab documentation, which can be shared via GitHub Pages under my Repo. With MKDocs, we will be adding the Material Theme alongside this, which is a popular site theme used on MKDoc sites.

For this deployment, we will be using Docker Compose. This setup will allow us to easily manage our project documentation, and check over its contents before moving over to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The container uses the host's SSH agent so that mkdocs gh-deploy can push to GitHub. For this to work, the SSH_AUTH_SOCK environment variable must reach Docker Compose.

By default, sudo resets the environment, which drops SSH_AUTH_SOCK and changes HOME to /root. It is recommended to add your user to the docker group and run Docker commands without sudo:

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER

Log out and back in for the group change to take effect. If you would rather keep using sudo, preserve both variables on each command instead:

sudo --preserve-env=SSH_AUTH_SOCK,HOME docker compose ...

docs.title: File Structure
docs.text:
Before we set up and run our Compose file, we first need to set up our folders where MKDocs will be installed.

For the main location of the MKDocs folder, I will be creating this under ~/pihomelab. This is also the root of the GitHub repository, so it holds the .git folder.

In this folder, we can create our configuration file mkdocs.yml, and enter the following starter config:

site_name: My Docs

nav:
  - Home: index.md
  - About: about.md

theme:
  name: 'material'

We can also create sub-folder docs, where all our .md files will be stored.

The finished folder will look like this:

~/pihomelab
├── .env                  # Local values, never committed
├── .gitignore
├── docs/
├── mkdocs.yml
└── mkdocs-compose.yaml

docs.title: SSH Agent Setup
docs.text:
SSH agent sockets normally live at a random, temporary path (e.g. /tmp/ssh-XXXXXXXXXXXX/agent.XXXXX) that is deleted when the SSH session ends. If a container is created with that path, it will fail to start once the session is gone (see Troubleshooting below).

To avoid this, we run the agent at a fixed path inside a dedicated folder, and mount that folder into the container rather than the socket file itself. Add the following to the end of ~/.bashrc:

# SSH agent at a fixed socket path (used by the MKDocs container)
export SSH_AUTH_SOCK="$HOME/.ssh-agent/agent.sock"
mkdir -p "$HOME/.ssh-agent" && chmod 700 "$HOME/.ssh-agent"
ssh-add -l >/dev/null 2>&1
if [ $? -eq 2 ]; then
  # Exit code 2 = no agent listening on the socket, so start a new one
  rm -f "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK"
  eval "$(ssh-agent -a "$SSH_AUTH_SOCK" -s)" >/dev/null
fi

Reload the shell and add your GitHub key to the agent:

source ~/.bashrc
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
ssh-add -l    # should list your key

The agent keeps running between SSH sessions, so new logins will reuse it. After a reboot, run ssh-add again to reload the key.

Make sure GitHub is in the host's known_hosts file, as this is mounted into the container so the push isn't blocked by a host key prompt:

ssh -T git@github.com

docs.title: Docker Compose File
docs.text:
For the compose file, we will be creating this under the ~/pihomelab folder, named mkdocs-compose.yaml. The following configuration will be used:

services:
  mkdocs:
    image: squidfunk/mkdocs-material
    container_name: mkdocs
    dns:
      - ${UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP}
      - ${PI_IP}
    networks:
      swarm_network:
    volumes:
      - ${MKDOCS_VOLUME}:/docs
      - ${HOME}/.ssh/known_hosts:/root/.ssh/known_hosts:ro
      - ${HOME}/.ssh-agent:/ssh-agent-dir
    environment:
      - SSH_AUTH_SOCK=/ssh-agent-dir/agent.sock
    stdin_open: true
    tty: true

networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true

Notes on this configuration: - No private keys in the container. Only known_hosts is mounted from ~/.ssh; authentication is handled by the agent. - The agent folder is mounted, not the socket. If the agent isn't running, the container still starts (pushes just won't authenticate until it is). - swarm_network is external, so driver and attachable are not set here. Those only apply when Compose creates the network itself. - ${HOME} is taken from your shell, so it does not need adding to .env. Run Compose as your own user (see Prerequisites) so it points to your home folder rather than /root.

The other variables are set in a .env file in the same folder as the compose file. Replace the placeholders with your own values:

MKDOCS_VOLUME=/home/<user>/pihomelab
UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP=<unbound container IP>
PI_IP=<raspberry pi IP>

Do not set SSH_AUTH_SOCK in .env. It is handled by ~/.bashrc and the compose file.

As ~/pihomelab is the repository, make sure .env is never pushed to GitHub by adding it to .gitignore:

echo ".env" >> ~/pihomelab/.gitignore

If .env was committed in the past, remove it from tracking with git rm --cached .env, then commit. Earlier commits will still contain it, so treat any values in it as public.

Inside ~/pihomelab, we can run the compose deployment command:

cd ~/pihomelab
docker compose -f mkdocs-compose.yaml up -d

We can confirm the container can see the agent and authenticate with GitHub:

docker exec -it mkdocs ssh-add -l
docker exec -it mkdocs ssh -T git@github.com

docs.title: Nginx Setup
docs.text:
Ensure its nginx server block is set up before proceeding, so that we can connect using its given local domain. As the compose file doesn't publish any ports, nginx reaches the container over swarm_network at http://mkdocs:8000.

We can test our deployment by connecting to the site, using example.com. Should be presented with the following:

![[Pasted image 20260826185955.png]]

docs.title: Updating MKDocs
docs.text:
As for all docker containers, please ensure that the containers are updated with the latest image!!

From ~/pihomelab, pull the latest image and recreate the container in one step:

docker compose -f mkdocs-compose.yaml pull
docker compose -f mkdocs-compose.yaml up -d

Compose will stop, remove and recreate the container only if the image has changed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Error: error mounting "/tmp/ssh-XXXXXXXXXXXX/agent.XXXXX" to rootfs at "/ssh-agent" ... not a directory

This happens on older versions of this setup, which mounted $SSH_AUTH_SOCK directly as a file. The container saved a temporary socket path from a previous SSH session; once that session ended, Docker recreated the missing path as a directory and could not mount it onto the /ssh-agent file inside the container.

To fix: 1. Check the stale path the container is using: 

docker inspect mkdocs --format '{{range .Mounts}}{{.Source}} -> {{.Destination}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'
2. Remove the empty directory Docker created (only if it is an empty directory, not a live socket), using the path shown above: 
sudo rm -rf /tmp/ssh-XXXXXXXXXXXX
3. Apply the SSH Agent Setup and compose file above, then recreate the container. docker start or docker compose start will reuse the old config, so it must be recreated: 
docker compose -f mkdocs-compose.yaml down
docker compose -f mkdocs-compose.yaml up -d --force-recreate

docs.title: 1. Installation for Pihole
docs.text: To install Pihole, we can use Docker Compose. This will allow us to use a .yaml file, which also contains the Unbound DNS container, that can work alongside Pihole.

docs.title: File Structures
docs.text:
As for the location of the yaml file, we will store this via ~/pihomelab/docker-compose, which will be where we are storing the docker compose files for all Docker services.

The data files and configs will be stored under ~/pihomelab/pihole (for Pihole) and ~/pihomelab/unbound for unbound. We also have the dnsmasq.d sub folder, which will be in the same location. This can be specified in the piholeunbound-compose.yaml file itself.

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text:
Any data and config files we don't want to share with the GitHub repo, will be added to the .gitignore file. This will include:

  • /pihole folder
  • /dnsmasq.d

docs.title: Docker Compose File
docs.text:
The following config is to be entered within the .yaml file:

services:
  pihole:
    container_name: pihole
    image: pihole/pihole:latest
    ports:
      - "53:53/tcp"
      - "53:53/udp"
    environment:
      TZ: ${TZ}  # Replace with your timezone
      FTLCONF_webserver_api_password: ${PIHOLE_PASSWORD}  # Change this!
      DNSMASQ_LISTENING: "all"
      PIHOLE_DNS_1: "unbound#53"  # Point to unbound container
    volumes:
      - ${PIHOLE_VOLUME}:/etc/pihole
      - ${DNSMASQ_VOLUME}:/etc/dnsmasq.d
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      swarm_network:
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
      - NET_RAW
      - CAP_SYS_NICE
      - CAP_SYS_TIME
    security_opt:
      - seccomp:unconfined
    depends_on:
      - unbound
  unbound:
    container_name: unbound
    image: klutchell/unbound:latest
    volumes:
      - ${UNBOUND_VOLUME}:/etc/unbound/custom.conf.d
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks:
      swarm_network:
networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true
    driver: overlay

ports: - Even though this is within our Docker Network, we still need to specify port 53 in this compose file, as this is the default port used for DNS. Without this, Pihole simply won't function as port 53 is not defined.

networks: - Our swarm_network is specified for connection.

docs.title: .env File
docs.text:
Note: For the password in this configuration, it is finding and using a created variable. We can just set a plain text password, but we can use this instead if sharing this config on GitHub, so it is hidden. To do this, create a new file in the same location named .env, and enter the following in it's file:

PIHOLE_PASSWORD=INSERT_HERE

INSERT_HERE can be replaced with the chosen password. .env is used, as GitHub is setup to ignore and not pull any .env files, as specified in it's .gitignore file, under ~/pihomelab.

docs.title: Deploying the compose file
docs.text:
Once this file(s) have been created, and config lines used above, we can then initiate it's installation via the following command:

sudo docker compose -f piholeunbound-compose.yaml up -d

Wait for the installation to finalise. Once finished, we can check that both the Unbound and Pihole containers are running via sudo docker ps.

docs.title: Updating Pihole/Unbound
docs.text:
As for all docker containers, please ensure that the containers are updated with the latest image!!

We can check if this is out of date, via the portal itself at the bottom of the page. This will note as Update Available.

Run the following command to pull the latest image, and then stopping and deleting the current containers, before installing again via the compose file:

docker pull pihole/pihole:latest
docker pull klutchell/unbound:latest

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text:
Nginx is a reverse proxy. It receives every request on ports 80 and 443, and forwards it to the right service based on the local domain entered (set up as local DNS records in Pihole).

Each service on the Raspberry Pi runs in its own Docker container. My previous Nginx setup ran on bare metal, outside Docker, which meant every service had to publish its own port on the Pi. For example, Pihole and Vaultwarden both default to port 80, so each needed a different host port. As this is all local, the ports aren't open to the public, but publishing one port per service is untidy and exposes more than needed.

Instead, Nginx and the other containers share one Docker network. Nginx reaches each container by its container name on the service's default port, so only Nginx needs ports 80 and 443 published on the Pi. For example, in a server block:

proxy_pass http://pihole:80;

Inside the shared network, containers can all use port 80 without clashing. A clash only happens when two containers try to publish the same port on the host.

docs.title: Docker Swarm and Network
docs.text:
Nginx runs as a Docker Swarm service on the Raspberry Pi, which is the swarm manager. Running it as a service lets it join the swarm_network overlay network, which spans every node, so it can also reach containers on other servers (e.g. Proxmox).

Creating the swarm and the swarm_network network is covered in the Portainer SWARM Setup guide, so make sure you're not duplicating networks. For reference, the network is created with:

# Creating a new external network for Portainer and all other containers to use
docker network create --driver overlay --attachable swarm_network

--attachable is required so that normal docker compose containers, not just swarm services, can join the network.

docs.title: Service File
docs.text:
The service file is saved as nginx-service.yaml under ~/pihomelab/docker-compose:

version: "3.8"
services:
  nginx:
    image: nginx:1.27  # pinned version, so updates are deliberate
    ports:
      # mode: host passes the real client IP to Nginx.
      # Without it, every request appears to come from the swarm ingress network.
      - target: 80
        published: 80
        protocol: tcp
        mode: host
      - target: 443
        published: 443
        protocol: tcp
        mode: host
    volumes:
      - ${NGINXVOLUME}:/etc/nginx/conf.d:ro
      - ${CERTSVOLUME}:/etc/openssl/certificates:ro
      - ${KEYSVOLUME}:/etc/openssl/keys:ro
    networks:
      - swarm_network
    deploy:
      replicas: 1
      placement:
        constraints:
          - node.role == manager # run on the Raspberry Pi
      restart_policy:
        condition: on-failure

networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true

A breakdown of the lines:

  • ports: publishes 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) on the Pi. These are the only ports clients need. Containers behind Nginx don't need their web ports published at all.
  • volumes: mounts the folders Nginx reads from. conf.d holds the server block files, and the certificates and keys folders hold the OpenSSL files created in 3. OpenSSL Self Signed Certificates. All are read-only (:ro).
  • networks: (inside the service) joins Nginx to swarm_network.
  • networks: (top level): external: true tells Docker the network already exists, so it doesn't try to create it. No driver line is needed for an external network.
  • deploy: holds swarm-only settings: one copy of Nginx, kept on the manager node (the Pi), restarted if it fails. If more manager nodes are added later, use node.hostname == [PI_HOSTNAME] to pin it to the Pi specifically.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
The volume paths are set in a .env file in the same folder. The names must match the service file exactly:

NGINXVOLUME=/home/[USER]/pihomelab/nginx
CERTSVOLUME=/etc/openssl/certificates
KEYSVOLUME=/etc/openssl/keys

Use full paths rather than ~, with no spaces around =.

docs.title: Shared Nginx Settings
docs.text:
Create 00-websocket.conf in the Nginx config folder (~/pihomelab/nginx, the NGINXVOLUME folder), alongside serverblock.conf. Every server block can then use these settings:

# Lets server blocks pass WebSocket connections through
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

# Docker's internal DNS, used to look up container names
resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=30s ipv6=off;

Note: This is an Nginx file, so it goes in the Nginx config folder, not Pihole's dnsmasq.d folder. Define the map and resolver only once. If serverblock.conf already has them, remove them from there.

Tip: With a plain proxy_pass http://pihole:80;, Nginx looks the container name up once at startup, and refuses to start if that container isn't running. Using a variable makes Nginx look it up per request through the resolver above, so one stopped container doesn't take down every site: 

set $upstream pihole;
proxy_pass http://$upstream:80;

docs.title: Deploying the Service
docs.text:
If the old standalone Nginx container is still running, remove it first, as it holds ports 80 and 443:

sudo docker compose -f nginx-compose.yaml down

docker stack deploy does not read .env files the way docker compose does. If the variables aren't loaded, the service deploys with empty volumes, and Nginx starts with no config, certificates or keys, so no domains work.

Load the variables into the shell first, then deploy. From ~/pihomelab/docker-compose:

set -a; . ./.env; set +a
docker stack deploy -c nginx-service.yaml proxy

This creates the service proxy_nginx. Running the same commands again later updates the existing service in place.

docs.title: Checking the Service
docs.text:
# Is it running, and on which node? (should be the Pi)
docker service ps proxy_nginx

# Did it get the right folders? Each line should show a full path
docker service inspect proxy_nginx --format '{{range .Spec.TaskTemplate.ContainerSpec.Mounts}}{{.Source}} -> {{.Target}}{{"\n"}}{{end}}'

# Logs. Look for "Configuration complete; ready for start up" with no [emerg] lines after it
docker service logs --tail 20 proxy_nginx

# Test the config files
docker exec $(docker ps -q -f name=proxy_nginx) nginx -t

After changing any config file, reload with:

docker service update --force proxy_nginx

To test a domain from the Pi (-L follows redirects, e.g. Pihole's /admin → /admin/login):

curl -kIL https://pihole.example.com/admin

docs.title: For Other Docker Containers Going Forward
docs.text:
Any container Nginx proxies to must be on swarm_network. Add this to its compose file:

services:
  myservice:
    container_name: myservice # the name Nginx uses in proxy_pass
    networks:
      - swarm_network

networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true

Its web port no longer needs publishing on the host. For Pihole, keep publishing port 53 (DNS), but remove 80:80, as the web interface is now reached through Nginx and port 80 belongs to Nginx.

swarm_network is the only network needed. Containers on it can also reach each other, so Pihole talks to Unbound over it too. Pihole's upstream field needs an IP rather than a container name, so set it to Unbound's IP on swarm_network:

docker inspect unbound --format '{{(index .NetworkSettings.Networks "swarm_network").IPAddress}}'

This IP can change if the Unbound container is recreated. To keep it fixed, give Unbound an ipv4_address under swarm_network in its compose file. This only works if the network was created with a set subnet, e.g. --subnet [SUBNET].

Any adjustments needed for specific services are covered in their own installation notes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No domains work, but the logs show no errors: the service was probably deployed with empty variables. Check the mounts with the docker service inspect command above, and redeploy with the variables loaded.
  • "This site can't be reached" in the browser, but curl works on the Pi: the device isn't resolving the domain through Pihole. Check for a VPN, or the browser's "Secure DNS" setting, both of which bypass Pihole.
  • 502 Bad Gateway on one domain: Nginx is fine, but it can't reach that container. Make sure the container is on swarm_network.

docs.title: 1. Portainer SWARM Setup
docs.text:
Portainer is a service used to manage our Docker containers through a web interface. This gives us options for viewing images, creating new containers, shutting down current ones, and so on.

However, with multiple servers, this gets harder to manage. You can create separate environments for each server, but if you want them to share the same Docker network, this isn't a viable solution.

docs.title: Docker Swarm
docs.text:
This is where Docker Swarm comes in. A Docker Swarm network allows containers to communicate with each other across multiple hosts (servers, or nodes), as if they were all on the same server or local network.

My current setup has two servers, Proxmox and Raspberry Pi, both of which host Docker containers. To set up one Docker network for all my containers, I can create a swarm with an overlay network, which Portainer can pick up and use.

You will need to decide which server will be the 'manager' of the swarm. In my case, I have picked my Raspberry Pi, as it hosts my main Docker containers, such as Nginx.

docs.title: Creating the Swarm
docs.text:
Once decided, we first need to initialise the swarm on that server, which makes it the manager:

# Initialise the swarm, making the current node manager
docker swarm init --advertise-addr eth0

This outputs a join command, which you can use later on another node. Example below:

# Output of command
docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-TOKEN [IP]:2377

docs.title: Creating the overlay network
docs.text:
Once the swarm is active, and the chosen server is confirmed as the manager, we can create the Docker network. This network will be used across all Docker Compose files, so that the containers are linked and can communicate with each other.

To do this, run the following command:

# Creating a new external network for Portainer and all other containers to use
docker network create --driver overlay --attachable swarm_network

Once created, we can use the following lines in Docker Compose files to include it:

services:
  myservice:
    networks:
      - swarm_network

networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true

The network has already been created as an overlay, so external: true is all that's needed. A driver line isn't required for an external network.

docs.title: Installing Portainer Stack
docs.text:
With the swarm and network set up, we can install the Portainer stack. A stack installs multiple Docker containers as a single application. This installation includes both the Portainer container and the agent.

First, grab the stack .yml from Portainer. Make sure this is done in your preferred location. For this example, it will be done under ~/pihomelab/docker-compose:

# Grabs the stack .yml
curl -L https://downloads.portainer.io/ce-lts/portainer-agent-stack.yml -o portainer-agent-stack.yml

docs.title: Docker Compose File
docs.text:
Edit this .yml to match the following:

# edit the downloaded yaml, to include the external network
version: '3.2'

services:
  agent:
    image: portainer/agent:lts
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - /var/lib/docker/volumes:/var/lib/docker/volumes
      - /:/host
    networks:
      - swarm_network
    dns:
      - ${UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP}
    deploy:
      mode: global
      placement:
        constraints: [node.platform.os == linux]

  portainer:
    image: portainer/portainer-ce:lts
    command: -H tcp://tasks.agent:9001 --tlsskipverify
    dns:
      - ${UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP}
    ports:
      - "9443:9443" # Web interface (HTTPS)
      - "9000:9000" # Web interface (HTTP)
      - "8000:8000" # Edge agent tunnel
    volumes:
      - portainer_data:/data
    networks:
      - swarm_network
    deploy:
      mode: replicated
      replicas: 1
      placement:
        constraints: [node.role == manager]

networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true

volumes:
  portainer_data:

Once entered and saved, deploy the stack. docker stack deploy doesn't read .env files, so load the variables first, otherwise UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP will be empty:

# Load the .env variables, then deploy the stack
set -a; . ./.env; set +a
docker stack deploy -c portainer-agent-stack.yml portainer

docs.title: Adding nodes
docs.text:
When the Portainer containers are active, we can request the join token from the manager node, and run the generated command on the new node so it joins the swarm.

# Obtain the docker swarm join token for a new node
docker swarm join-token worker

# Run the command generated above on the other server
docker swarm join --token SWMTKN-1-TOKEN [IP]:[PORT]

docs.title: 1. RClone Setup
docs.text:
With the current setup (pre-NAS Server), I have been using RClone, which can be used to backup chosen folders of data from the Raspberry Pi, and upload to a Cloud Service. For my chosen Cloud Service, I have decided to use Proton Drive.

Note: This was done as the root user, using command sudo su

To start, we can first install RClone via the following command:

sudo -v ; curl https://rclone.org/install.sh | sudo bash

Once installed, we will need to proceed on setting up the config. This will trigger prompts for setting up our backups to the Cloud Service:

rclone config

Proceed with the following options:

  1. Enter n to start a new remote.
  2. This will prompt for a name. I have entered 'ProtonDrive'.
  3. We will then need to pick our Cloud Service. Choose 43 for Proton Drive.
  4. For this service, enter the email address used for the Cloud Service Login.
  5. Choose the option for entering your password to the Cloud Service Account.
  6. Enter the 2FA code tied to your Cloud Service Account (6-digit Code).
  7. Do not enter a secret key, or editing the advanced config when prompted.

Once the setup is complete, run the command below to check that RClone is picking up the Cloud Service folders present on the account:

rclone lsd ProtonDrive:

For example, in my Proton Drive, I have folder 'Raspberry Pi Backups' present, which this command outputs.

We can now proceed on creating the backup script. I have navigated to /etc/backups, where this script will sit. The following is set inside of file backupscr.sh:

#!/bin/bash

# ==== Configuration ====
REMOTE_NAME="ProtonDrive"
DESTINATION_BASE="Raspberry Pi Backups"
SOURCES=( "/home/user" "/etc/" ) #The two folders we want to back up
TIMESTAMP=$(date +"%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S")
DESTINATION="$REMOTE_NAME:$DESTINATION_BASE/$TIMESTAMP"
FILELIST="/tmp/rclone_files.txt"
# =======================

# Clear previous file list
> "$FILELIST"

echo "Starting backup to: $DESTINATION"

# Collect all files from each source folder
for SRC in "${SOURCES[@]}"; do
    if [ -d "$SRC" ]; then
        find "$SRC" -type f >> "$FILELIST"
        echo "Added files from: $SRC"
    else
        echo "Warning: $SRC is not a valid folder. Skipping."
    fi
done

# Run rclone to copy the files while preserving full paths
rclone copy / "$DESTINATION" \
    --files-from "$FILELIST" \
    --create-empty-src-dirs \
    --copy-links \
    --progress

echo "Backup finished!"

This backs up both the /etc/ folder, and the /home/user/ folder. To make this script executable, run the following:

sudo chmod +x backupscr.sh

You can then run this manually via the following command:

./your_script_name.sh

docs.title: 1. Router DDNS & Port Forwarding
docs.text:
Before we get started, we need to setup our router for port forwarding on port 51820, and enabling DDNS.

  • A Dynamic DNS service is used to automatically update the IP Address if and when it changes. This is useful to use for our VPN, as if the Router reboots, we won't need to manually update the public IP again for our VPN to use.
  • Port forwarding allow us to open port 51820, so that we can connect through to the local network via this.

These steps will go through the ASUS Router settings.

docs.title: Port Forward
docs.text:
Log into your router dashboard, usually being 192.168.x.1.

On the dashboard, under Advanced Settings, click WAN > Virtual Server / Port Forwarding.

The page will show a table of where your port forwarded ports will show. Press Add Profile, and fill in the following information:

![[Pasted image 20260820180307.png]]

Service Name - Name of your choosing Protocol - BOTH External Port - 51820 Internal IP Address - localserver IP of where your PiVPN service will be hosted on Press OK to confirm settings.

docs.title: DDNS Service
docs.text:
On the same router dashboard, navigate to WAN > DDNS. On this page, we can fill in the following details:

  • DDNS - Toggle ON
  • Server - WWW.ASUS.COM
  • Host name - Name of your choosing (.asuscomm.com)
  • HTTPS/SSL Certificate - Auto

Then press Apply.

We can check if this has applied and registered successfully, checking under Network Map > Internet Status > DDNS name

docs.title: 2. Configuration Files & HTTP
docs.text:
To begin configuring Nginx, we need to understand its file structure. In the Nginx service file, the volume /etc/nginx/conf.d points at a folder in our home directory, which for me is ~/pihomelab/nginx (the NGINXVOLUME path in .env). The main Nginx configuration file, nginx.conf, already exists inside the container under /etc/nginx. We won't see or need to edit it, as it automatically loads every .conf file in conf.d.

Any additional config files, mainly our proxy server block file, are added to the folder set in the volume, which the Nginx container reads from.

For this setup, we only need to create a .conf file containing our server block proxy configuration. CD into your chosen folder and create the .conf file, choosing a name that suits you. My file is named serverblock.conf.

cd ~/pihomelab/nginx
nano serverblock.conf

Note: Files must end in .conf, otherwise Nginx ignores them. Creating them without sudo keeps them owned by your user, so they can be edited later without permission errors.

docs.title: Server Block Example
docs.text:
For a basic HTTP setup for our Pihole service, we can use the following template:

server {
    listen 80;
    server_name example.com www.example.com; # Replace with your domain

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://pihole:80; # Backend container name/port
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

On the proxy_pass line, we only need to give pihole, the name of the Docker container, rather than an IP address. Port 80 is added, as this is the default port Pihole uses. This works because Nginx and Pihole are both on swarm_network.

Tip: As covered in 1. Installation, using set $upstream pihole; with proxy_pass http://$upstream:80; stops Nginx failing to start if the Pihole container isn't running.

With the lines added, save the file and test the configuration for syntax errors. Nginx runs as the swarm service proxy_nginx, so the command is run inside its container with docker exec:

docker exec $(docker ps -q -f name=proxy_nginx) nginx -t

If all is good, reload Nginx to apply the changes:

docker exec $(docker ps -q -f name=proxy_nginx) nginx -s reload

If the reload doesn't pick up the changes, restart the service instead:

docker service update --force proxy_nginx

docs.title: 2. Initial Web Interface Setup
docs.text:
Once Portainer is up and running, we can load up the webpage using the domain setup on Nginx. This will bring up the setup page.

On the setup page, enter your username, and a password to set again the account. For the setup token, you can obtain this by running the docker logs command for the portainer container:

docker logs portainer

In the logs, it will show the setup token, which you can copy and paste into and accept.

The primary environment should already be setup. You can click on this under the 'Environments' tab. To confirm Swarm is running correctly, and that your node appears in the list, click on the 'Swarm' tab on the navigation menu under the environment, and choose 'Details'

Here, you should see two nodes, one being your primary manager, and the other being the one you joined the swarm with.

docs.title: 2. Installation for PiVPN
docs.text:
Pivpn is a easy-to-use script we can run, that will allow us to install our chosen VPN Protocols. In this case, we will be installing Wireguard via this script. This Wireguard VPN will allow us to access the services hosted on our Pi, as well as the Proxmox server, from outside of the local network. This will connect us to the network, as if we're a device within the network.

PLEASE NOTE: This guide assumes you have already setup Pihole + Unbound. If not, please refer to [1. Installation].

docs.title: Installation Command
docs.text:
To get started, we can simply run the installation command here:

curl -L https://install.pivpn.io | bash
  • If sudo apt update has not been ran beforehand, this will automatically run, and update any packages available.

docs.title: GUI Steps
docs.text:
This will initiate a GUI Installation. Follow through the prompts as below:

  1. Press OK

  2. Press OK - We already have static IP address 192.164.x.x set.

  3. Select Yes, as this is still a good idea so that it stops private data from leaking if it uses ipv6 in the future.

  4. Press space on eth0, which is the Ethernet connection used for the Pi. If using Wi-Fi, select WAN, and press OK.

  5. Press Yes, as DCHP Reservation is being used for IP 192.168.x.x.

  6. Press OK, and select user or the main local account you're using for the Pi.

  7. Select Wireguard using the spacebar, and press OK.

  8. Stick with port 51820, and press Ok (We will ensure this is port forwarded on the Router config later on) then Confirm.

  9. Select PiVPN-is-local-DNS by using the spacebar, and pressing OK. As noted, as we're using unbound, we should select this option.

  10. Choose DNS Entry.

  11. Enter the domain name that we set earlier under [1. Router DDNS & Port Forwarding]. This will be x.asuscomm.com.

  12. We will then have confirmation that the server keys will be generated. Press OK.

  13. This will recommend enabling unattended-upgrades. We can confirm, and press Yes, as this is an important feature to enable for automatic security package updates.

  14. This will then confirm the installation has complete. Press OK, and press Yes to confirm reboot.

We can then move on to creating our client.

docs.title: Adding the .md files
docs.text:
The .md files are called from the docs folder inside ~/pihomelab/docs. We can either create .md files from scratch, or create and transfer them over into the folder.

I have created my .md files via an note taking application called Obsidian, and transferred these over. These were copied over using the SSH application MobaXTerm, by simply dragging them over to the file structure tab.

I ran the command below, so that I had the correct write permissions for copying across:

sudo chmod -R 777 ~/pihomelab/docs

docs.title: 2. Project Repository Setup
docs.text: Next, we want to create our repository on Github. These steps were used to create my public repository Pi-Homelab as part of my Raspberry Pi Project, as user f0oney.

docs.title: GitHub Repository Creation
docs.text:
Firstly, we want to create a new repository via Github. Login to the Github main homepage, and click New. This opens the new Github repository page. Fill in the details, and set this to private for the time being.

Repository for the Raspberry Pi Homelab is named Pi-Homelab, and linked here: https://github.com/f0oney/Pi-Homelab

Once created, we can then move over to the Raspberry Pi, to create our project repo folder, where we will link this across to the created GitHub Repo.

docs.title: Repo folder structure on Server/Device
docs.text:
On your device, under /home/user/, we can create a new folder named after your project. For this example, we can user PiProject, via the following command:

sudo mkdir pihomelab
cd /home/home/pihomelab

Inside of this folder, we can then run the git command below, to create the repo files:

sudo git init -b main

Once the git files have been created, we can start structuring this repo folder, by adding in the separate folders for each of your services. For me, I have vaultwarden and pihole-unbound that I can add in as sub-folders:

sudo mkdir -p ~/pihomelab/vaultwarden
sudo mkdir -p ~/pihomelab/pihole
sudo mkdir -p ~/pihomelab/unbound

docs.title: .gitignore
docs.text:
We can then create a .gitignore file, which allows us to specify files we do not want to have show up under our GitHub repository. These can include .env files, or .db files to name a couple.

sudo nano .gitignore

I have then entered the following file types (* meaning any word used):

.env *.env *.db *.sqlite *.sqlite-journal

You can add folders etc, which I have additionally done, to hide the sensitive data and configs.

docs.title: Remote Origin
docs.text:
Next step is to add the remote origin, that links to our private repository created in GitHub, via the following:

sudo git remote add origin git@github.com:username/reponame.git

docs.title: Stage and Commits
docs.text:
Once satisfied, we then want to stage the current structure and updates done to this project folder:

git add .

This can then be followed by commiting the changes, so that it saves it locally:

sudo git commit -m "Initial homelab setup and folder structure"
- The comment in the speech marks adds a comment on the github page, once the changes have been made.

docs.title: Push
docs.text:
We can then finally push these files and changes to the GitHub repository, by using the push command:

sudo git push -u origin main
- This pushes it to the main branch of the repository. - Command will prompt for github username, but also the github password. - The Github password will require you to create a Personal Token Key within the Developer settings of GitHub. Recommend generating a classic token key, and then copying this into the console.

Tip: We can add --force, if there is already a README folder in, that we are happy with replacing when the pull command is initiated.

docs.title: 2. Schedule using Crontab
docs.text:
I've set crontab to run every Saturday, at 3AM, using the backup script located in /home/fooney/raspberrypi-homelab/. Done this by:

Crontab - e

Press option 1

In the file, we've added the following line:

0 3 * * 6 /home/user/pihomelab/backupscr.sh

These parameters state it will run every week, on a Saturday. We can use the following website that will help show which parameters we will need to use:

https://crontab.guru/#0_3___6

The following explains each part of the syntax:

  • 1: Minute (between 0 and 59)
  • 2: Hour (between 0 and 23)
  • 3: Day (between 1 and 31)
  • 4: Month (between 1 and 12)
  • 5: Day of week (between 0 and 7, starting on Sunday)

docs.title: 2. Unbound Config Files
docs.text:
Once the containers are installed, we can then proceed on creating the Unbound files. These aren't necessary, due to the container already pre-generating these in the background, but we can create these manually under ~/pihomelab/unbound if we want to edit and create custom configs.

These will then mirror over to /etc/unbound/custom.conf.d, as directed on the directory setting of Unbound on the .yaml file - [[Raspberry Pi/Pihole & Unbound/1. Installation|1. Installation]]. Then, any files mirror'd to custom.conf.d, Unbound will pick up, and use over it's default configs.

Firstly, lets ensure the /etc/unbound/custom.conf.d folder exists on the system. If not already, cd to /etc/, and enter the following commands:

cd /etc/
mkdir unbound
cd unbound/
mkdir custom.conf.d

We will then need to cd over to ~/pihomelab/unbound, and can create the following files...

docs.title: unbound.conf
docs.text:
sudo nano unbound.conf

server:
    verbosity: 1
    interface: 0.0.0.0 # Listening on all network interfaces, so it can accept traffic coming in from the Docker bridge network 172.x.x.x
    port: 53
    do-ip4: yes
    do-udp: yes
    do-tcp: yes

    # May be set to yes if you have IPv6 connectivity
    do-ip6: yes

    # Use this only when you downloaded the list of primary root servers!
    root-hints: /etc/unbound/custom.conf.d/root.hints

    # Trust glue only if it is within the servers authority
    harden-glue: yes

    # Require DNSSEC data for trust-anchored zones, if no DNSSEC data for an answer,
    # with trust anchors enabled, the zone becomes Bogus
    harden-dnssec-stripped: yes

    # Don't use capitalization randomization
    use-caps-for-id: no

    # Reduce EDNS reassembly buffer size
    edns-buffer-size: 1472

    # Perform prefetching of close to expired message cache entries
    prefetch: yes

    # Min and Max time DNS Records are cached for, in seconds
    cache-min-ttl: 3600
    cache-max-ttl: 86400

    # One thread should be sufficient
    num-threads: 1

    # Ensure kernel buffer is large enough (reduced to avoid permission warnings)
    so-rcvbuf: 400k

    # Respond to queries from local networks only
    access-control: 127.0.0.0/8 allow
    access-control: 10.0.0.0/8 allow
    access-control: 172.16.0.0/12 allow
    access-control: 192.168.0.0/16 allow

    # Ensure privacy of local IP ranges
    private-address: 192.168.0.0/16
    private-address: 169.254.0.0/16
    private-address: 172.16.0.0/12
    private-address: 10.0.0.0/8
    private-address: fd00::/8
    private-address: fe80::/10

.                        3600000      NS    F.ROOT-SERVERS.NET.
F.ROOT-SERVERS.NET.      3600000      A     192.5.5.241
F.ROOT-SERVERS.NET.      3600000      AAAA  2001:500:2f::f
;
; FORMERLY NS.NIC.DDN.MIL
;
.                        3600000      NS    G.ROOT-SERVERS.NET.

It is recommended to update the root.hints file once every 6 months, as domains may update by InterNic. We can simply use the second command above to re-generate the file and it's contents.

docs.title: dnsmaq.d
docs.text:
We can also configure and create our custom configuration file for dnsmasq. This is located in ~/pihomelab/dnsmaq.d, which we can cd into, and run command sudo nano 02-lan-access.conf, entering the following config:

# Allow all interfaces
listen-address=0.0.0.0
bind-interfaces
domain-needed
bogus-priv
EOF

docs.title: resolv.conf
docs.text:
To prevent DNS leaks, we can set resolv.conf to use Pihole, and also ensure it is immutable so that we prevent the DHCP from changing it:

echo "nameserver 127.0.0.1" | sudo tee /etc/resolv.conf
sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf

docs.title: dhclient
docs.text:
We can set in the dhclient.conffile to point to domain server 127.0.0.1:

sudo nano /etc/dhcp/dhclient.conf

#Add in the file
supersede domain-name-servers 127.0.0.1;

docs.title: Docker DNS
docs.text:
We will also need to configure the Docker DNS via the daemon.json file. To do this, create or edit /etc/docker/daemon.json

sudo nano /etc/docker/daemon.json

#Add in the file
{
    "dns": ["127.0.0.1"]
}

docs.title: 3. Backups
docs.text:
As we're hosting our password manager locally, sometimes, we may lose this data under unfortunate circumstances. Therefore, it is important to backup our password database, so that if anything did happen to the server for example, we have backups readily available.

For the method I am using, I will be setting up Rclone (the same service used for our system file backups) and the vaultwarden-backup docker contianer.

docs.title: Updated vaultwarden-compose.yaml file
docs.text:
In order to do this for vaultwarden, we will be making use of another docker container. This will be added on to our existing docker compose file for Vaultwarden. The following can be added:

services:
  vaultwarden:
    image: vaultwarden/server:latest
    container_name: vaultwarden
    restart: unless-stopped
    dns:
      - ${UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP} # To ensure Vaultwarden uses Unbound (Docker IP)
      - ${PI_IP} # Fallback to Pi IP as DNS
    networks:
      swarm_network:
    environment:
      DOMAIN: ${DOMAIN}  # enter your domain
      SIGNUPS_ALLOWED: "false"                  # disable after creating your first account
      ADMIN_TOKEN: ${ARGON2_HASH}
    volumes:
      - ${VAULTWARDEN_VOLUME}:/data

  backup:
      image: ttionya/vaultwarden-backup:latest
      container_name: vaultwarden-backup
      restart: unless-stopped
      dns:
        - ${UNBOUND_DOCKER_IP} # To ensure Vaultwarden uses Unbound (Docker IP)
        - ${PI_IP} # Fallback to Pi IP as DNS
      networks:
        swarm_network:
      environment:
        # Must match the remote created with rclone config
        RCLONE_REMOTE_NAME: "BitwardenBackup"

        # Directory inside the remote storage
        RCLONE_REMOTE_DIR: "/Vaultwarden Backups/"

        # Run at the start of every month
        CRON: "0 0 1 * *"

        # Create one encrypted archive
        ZIP_ENABLE: "TRUE"
        ZIP_TYPE: "7z"
        ZIP_PASSWORD: ${ARGON2_HASH_BACKUP}

        # Keep backups from the last 30 days
        BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS: "30"

        # Optional: use your local timezone
        TIMEZONE: ${TZ}

        # Optional: identify this server in logs and notifications
        DISPLAY_NAME: "vaultwarden"

      volumes:
        - ${VAULTWARDEN_VOLUME}:/bitwarden/data/
        - vaultwarden-rclone-data:/config/

volumes:
  vaultwarden-rclone-data:
    external: true
    name: vaultwarden-rclone-data

networks:
  swarm_network:
    external: true
    driver: overlay

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: The following variables have been used, and described as so:

docs.title: backup service
docs.text: The main backup service is used, pulling it's image, setting it's container_name, and also calling the dns server IPs and docker network dns_network.

docs.title: RCLONE
docs.text: RCLONE_REMOTE_NAME will be the Rclone connection name that we will be calling from the set volume. RCLONE_REMOTE_DIR will be the location of the backups within our Cloud Drive. This case being on Proton Drive.

docs.title: CRON
docs.text:
This will set when the backup runs via crontab. Example being running everyday, at 2:30AM:

0 4 * * *

docs.title: ZIP
docs.text: The variable ZIP_ENABLE allows the backup to be encrypted, using the other variable ZIP_TYPE to set it's file type, and ZIP_PASSWORD being the password used to access it.

docs.title: BACKUP_KEEP_DAYS
docs.text: This singular variable will determine how long the backup exists for, before being removed.

docs.title: Volume
docs.text: The volume vaultwarden-rclone-date is created, and marked as external, as it will be already created outside of the docker compose file, with data already setup.

docs.title: Volume Creation
docs.text:
To create our volume outside of the Docker Compose File, we can run the following command:

docker volume create vaultwarden-rclone-data

Once it exists as a volume, we can then setup our Rclone configuration. This will allow us to setup what cloud service we will be using:

docker run --rm -it \
  --mount type=volume,source=vaultwarden-rclone-data,target=/config/ \
  ttionya/vaultwarden-backup:latest \
  rclone config

Proceed with the following options:

  1. Enter n to start a new remote.
  2. This will prompt for a name. I have entered 'ProtonDrive'.
  3. We will then need to pick our Cloud Service. Choose 43 for Proton Drive.
  4. For this service, enter the email address used for the Cloud Service Login.
  5. Choose the option for entering your password to the Cloud Service Account.
  6. Do not enter a 2FA code.
  7. Enter the secret key (OTP) of your authenticator. This can typically be found on your authenticator app. This is so that it does not rely on your cached authenticator code, as once lost, you have to reset the authentication login.
  8. Press No on advanced setup

Once setup, we can simply exit out of the configuration using q. To confirm this has been setup correctly, we can run the following:

docker run --rm -it \
  --mount type=volume,source=vaultwarden-rclone-data,target=/config/ \
  ttionya/vaultwarden-backup:latest \
  rclone config show

Once happy, we can then run our compose file. Please ensure that the current vaultwarden container has been stopped and deleted.

sudo docker compose -f vaultwarden-compose.yaml up -d

docs.title: 3. Create a Client
docs.text: A client is essentially a individual tunnel that you can use to connect your device to the local network. It is heavily recommended to create separate clients for each device. This example will walk through creating one for my laptop.

docs.title: Client Process
docs.text:
To start creating one, simply run the command below:

pivpn -a

This will prompt to enter the Client IP from range. You can either enter one yourself, or press enter to let Pivpn pick one for you:

::: Chosen Client IP: random IP

It will then ask for the name of the client. You will receive confirmation that this has been created successfully.

docs.title: Adding Tunnel to the Wireguard Mobile App
docs.text:
We can use command pivpn -qr, and enter the client name, to generate the QR of the client. This can be scanned from the Wireguard Phone App.

To do this, open the Wireguard app and press the + symbol, selecting Scan from QR code. This should then add the tunnel to your app for use.

docs.title: Adding Tunnel to the Wireguard Desktop App
docs.text:
To add the tunnel to your Desktop app, we will need to physically save the .conf file of the client, and add to the application. These client .conf files are located in /home/user/configs.

To download this file onto our laptop, I am using application MobaXTerm, which will let me physically right-click the file within the file directory pane, and press Download:

![[Pasted image 20260819222725.png]]

Once downloaded, we can open Wireguard and navigate through the following:

  1. Click Add Tunnel
  2. Locate the saved .conf file, and double-click to open
  3. You should then see the tunnel appear on your list. Press Activate to start up the VPN.

docs.title: 3. Deploying to Github Pages
docs.text:
As MKDocs is running in a container, mkdocs gh-deploy needs to be run inside the container. This is done with docker exec, followed by the container name (mkdocs, as set by container_name in the compose file) and the command itself:

docker exec mkdocs mkdocs gh-deploy

The container authenticates with GitHub through the host's SSH agent, which is set up in 1. Installation for MkDocs (SSH Agent Setup and Docker Compose File). Complete those sections before continuing.

docs.title: Check the Repository Remote
docs.text:
gh-deploy pushes to whichever remote the repository uses. For the SSH agent to be used, the remote must be an SSH URL (git@github.com:...) rather than HTTPS. On the host, from the repository folder:

cd ~/pihomelab
git remote -v

If it shows an https:// URL, switch it to SSH:

git remote set-url origin git@github.com:<username>/<repo>.git

The container only sees the folder mounted at /docs (MKDOCS_VOLUME, i.e. ~/pihomelab). As this is the repository root, the .git folder is included and the container can find the repository. If MKDOCS_VOLUME is ever pointed at a sub-folder instead, gh-deploy will fail with not a git repository.

docs.title: Check the Host SSH Agent
docs.text:
Confirm the agent is running and holds your key. After a reboot, the key needs to be added again:

ssh-add -l
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519   # only if no key is listed

docs.title: Verify the Container Can See the Agent
docs.text:
Confirm the known_hosts file and the agent socket are mounted, and that the agent is reachable from inside the container:

docker exec mkdocs ls -la /root/.ssh /ssh-agent-dir
docker exec mkdocs ssh-add -l

The second command should list the same key as on the host.

docs.title: Test GitHub Authentication Inside the Container
docs.text:
Verify that the container can authenticate against GitHub using the agent:

docker exec mkdocs ssh -T git@github.com

Expected response: Hi username! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

docs.title: Deploy the Documentation
docs.text:
Build the site and push it to the repository's gh-pages branch:

docker exec mkdocs mkdocs gh-deploy --force

--force overwrites the gh-pages branch with the new build. This is safe as long as nothing else commits to that branch. gh-deploy also adds the .nojekyll file to the branch automatically, so GitHub Pages serves the built HTML as-is.

Only the docs folder is built into the site, so .env and mkdocs-compose.yaml are not published to GitHub Pages. They are still part of the repository itself, which is why .env is listed in .gitignore (see 1. Installation for MkDocs).

docs.title: Configure GitHub Pages
docs.text:
This only needs doing once. In the repository on GitHub, go to Settings → Pages, and under Build and deployment set: - Source: Deploy from a branch - Branch: gh-pages, folder / (root)

The site will be published at https://<username>.github.io/<repo>/ after a short delay.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
fatal: detected dubious ownership in repository at '/docs'

The container runs as root, while the files belong to your user on the host, so Git refuses to use the repository. Mark the folder as safe inside the container:

docker exec mkdocs git config --global --add safe.directory /docs

This setting is lost when the container is recreated (e.g. after an image update), so re-run it if the error returns.

Permission denied (publickey)

The container can't reach the agent, or the agent has no key loaded. Re-run the checks in "Check the Host SSH Agent" and "Verify the Container Can See the Agent". If ssh-add -l works on the host but not in the container, recreate the container so it picks up the agent folder mount:

cd ~/pihomelab
docker compose -f mkdocs-compose.yaml up -d --force-recreate

docs.title: 3. OpenSSL Self Signed Certificates
docs.text:
OpenSSL is the service we will use to create our certificates, which will allow us to use HTTPS against our local domains. OpenSSL is recommended for self-signed certificates, as noted by Lets Encrypt via their Documentation.

'Self-Signed' certificates are certificates signed by the creator's own private key, rather then a trusted third-party Certificate Authority. This allows us to complete this completely offline, whilst having the basic encryption needed for our web portals.

The downside to this setup however, is that we would need to manually download the certificate onto each device, and add to the web browser being used. This means that the certificates are not trusted by anyone else, but for local development, this is fine.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To get started, we can install OpenSSL via the following command:

sudo apt install openssl

docs.title: Folder Structures
docs.text:
Once installed, we next need to create a folder where we will store the certificates. In this case, I will be creating a folder named openssl under /etc/openssl:

cd /etc/
mkdir openssl
cd /etc/openssl

In the folder, we can begin running our commands to create the certificates.

docs.title: Creating the Certificates
docs.text:
Firstly, we will need to create the key for the CA Certificate. This will be named userCA.key. The following command is ran below:

openssl genrsa -des3 -out userCA.key 4096

Then, we will need to generate the CA certificate itself with the created CA key, named userCA.crt. This will prompt for the information required for the certificate…

openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -key userCA.key -out userCA.crt

The info it requests will be as follows:

  • Country Name (2 letter code)
  • State or Province Name
  • City
  • Organisation Name
  • Organisational Unit Name
  • Common Name (e.g. server FQDN or YOUR name)
  • Email Address

The information does not need to be real, and you can enter fake information, such as a fake name. This is because no public authority checks these.

Once the CA root certificate is created, we can then proceed with creating the wildcard custom domain certificate. This allows us to use the certificate for any local domains using *.user.local, named user.key:

openssl genrsa -out user.key 2048

We will now need to create the config file openssl.cnf, which we are going to use for CSR and signing. The CSR is a Certificate Signing Request, which is a message sent to the CA (Certificate Authority) to apply for a certificate. To create and start the config file, we can run:

Sudo nano openssl.conf

Then, the following can be entered in the config file itself:

[req]
default_md = sha256
prompt = no
req_extensions = req_ext
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name

[req_distinguished_name]
commonName = *.example.com
countryName = YOUR_COUNTRY
stateOrProvinceName = No state
localityName = No City
organizationName = No Company

[req_ext]
keyUsage=critical,digitalSignature,keyEncipherment
extendedKeyUsage=critical,serverAuth,clientAuth
subjectAltName = @alt_names

[alt_names]
DNS.1=user.local
DNS.2=*.user.local

We can then use this to create the CSR:

openssl req -new -nodes -key user.key -config openssl.cnf -out user.csr

We can finally then sign this with the created CA. The final certificate that we can use will be named user.crt:

openssl x509 -req -in user.csr -CA userCA.crt -CAkey userCA.key -CAcreateserial -out user.crt -days 1024 -sha256 -extfile openssl.cnf -extensions req_ext

With the certificates and keys created, we can organise these into sub folders within the OpenSSL folder:

/etc/openssl/ca_certificates userCA.crt /etc/openssl/ca_keys userCA.key /etc/openssl/certificates user.crt /etc/openssl/keys user.key

docs.title: Installing the Certificates
docs.text:
For us to be able to use these on our devices, we will need to install them on each individual device. As I am using MobaXTerm for accessing the Pi console via SSH, I can simply navigate to the file directory via the file directory tree (found on the left side of the application).

We want to install the userCA.crt certificate on the device, via /etc/openssl/ca_certificates, by highlighting the file > right-click > press Download.

Once this is on our machine, we can then share this on other devices by any preferable method. The steps on installing the certificate is slightly different however.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: We can simply follow the steps found under #Trusted-Root-CA, on [[Router HTTPS Configuration]]. This will guide you on how to add the certificate to the Trusted Root Certification Authorities.

docs.title: Android
docs.text:
Under the settings, navigate through the following settings:

  1. Click on Security and privacy > More security settings > Install from device storage > CA certificate
  2. Choose Install anyway
  3. Enter your device password or biometrics
  4. Find the file in your storage, and click Done

docs.title: Browser
docs.text:
We can also add it to our browsers, via it's certificate settings. Steps vary depending on browser, but for Firefox, this can be done via:

  1. Click on Privacy and Security
  2. Choose Advanced settings under Connection and software security
  3. Scroll down to Certificates, and choose Manage Certificates
  4. Press Import, and select the certificate stored on your device

docs.title: 3. Router DNS Configuration
docs.text: With Pihole + Unbound now setup, we lastly need to make sure that all devices connected to the local network, is using this configuration as it's DNS. Currently, all devices will still use the default router's DNS settings, so therefore, Pihole with Unbound is completely bypassed. To change this, we will need to go onto the router's portal and amend it.

docs.title: Router Steps
docs.text:
For my setup, I have obtained a third party router, specifically model RT-AX52 Pro by ASUS. I had to purchase one of these, to allow me to add custom configurations for DNS, as well as other features and settings I would not get with my default router provided by my ISP, due to custom configurations being locked down.

  1. Firstly, login to your router via it's local IP on the browser, usually 192.168.0.1. For ASUS, it will prompt for my username and password which I set in it's setup.
  2. Once logged in, navigate to LAN under Advanced Settings, and then click on the DHCP Server Tab.
  3. Look for fields DNS Server 1 and DNS Server 2, under DNS and WINS Server Setting.
  4. On both these fields, enter the Raspberry Pi's IP Address, where Pihole and Unbound is hosted on. Again, this will usually be something like 192.168.0.x.

![[Pasted image 20260817213054.png]]

  • We want both servers set to this, so that it does not have any chance in using another DNS Server.

  • Press Apply. This will reboot the router, and apply the changes.

The networks DNS should now use the Raspberry Pi's IP, which both Pihole and Unbound are hosted on, and direct all queries to this going forward. Any device on the network will therefore use this going forward.

docs.title: 3. Shared Repository Files
docs.text:
Inside of ~/pihomelab, this will be our main folder for all our docker services. We need to be careful with how we do this however, as we do not want to share sensitive information such as API keys and config files that should not be on our Github repo.

It is important therefore to ensure that we are adding any folders/files into the .gitignore folder, so that they are properly hidden.

docs.title: 4. HTTPS Configuration
docs.text:
With the self-signed certificates created, we can use them to set up HTTPS connections to our local domains. For this example, we will add HTTPS to the Pihole server block we set up previously.

Open the server block created earlier with nano ~/pihomelab/nginx/serverblock.conf, and add the following:

server {
    listen 443 ssl; # https port
    listen [::]:443 ssl; # used for ipv6
    server_name example.com www.example.com;

    ssl_certificate /etc/openssl/certificates/user.crt; # location of the certs
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/openssl/keys/user.key; # location of the keys

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://pihole:80; # Backend container name/port
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key tell Nginx where to find the certificate and key for the connection. These paths are inside the container, mounted from the CERTSVOLUME and KEYSVOLUME folders set in .env.

listen 443 ssl replaces port 80, as 443 is the HTTPS port.

listen [::]:443 ssl does the same for IPv6 connections. Both lines need ssl, otherwise that listener serves plain HTTP.

To redirect HTTP requests to HTTPS, add the following server block above it:

server {
    listen 80; # http port
    listen [::]:80; # used for ipv6

    server_name example.com www.example.com;
    return 301 https://example.com/admin;
}

With the Pihole server block now complete, check for syntax errors before applying the changes:

docker exec $(docker ps -q -f name=proxy_nginx) nginx -t
docker exec $(docker ps -q -f name=proxy_nginx) nginx -s reload

For the other server blocks set up for the Raspberry Pi services, see the Server Block Service Examples section.

docs.title: 4. Pihole Web Interface Login & Checks
docs.text: Next, is logging into the Pihole Interface, and a quick overview of what we can do, and the settings available to us.

docs.title: IP & Local Domain
docs.text:
To first load up the Pihole Interface, we will need to enter your IP Address in the Address Bar. Example being: http://192.168.x.x:${PORT}

With Nginx, we can set this up against a local domain, something like https://pihole.user.local, with HTTPS enabled with self-signed certs. You can find how these were setup via [Insert guide links], but for the time being, after initial setup without Nginx and Self-Signed Certs, the IP Address mentioned above will allow you onto the login page with HTTP.

docs.title: Main Portal Page
docs.text:
Once loaded, we will be presented with the login page. Enter the password setup from the installation guide [1. Installation], which was set on the compose file.

![[Pasted image 20260815162538.png|394]]

Once logged in, we will be presented with the main dashboard. This will show the current status, total queries made, queries blocked, and client activity. We can also view the Upstream Servers widget, which shows which servers are actioning the queries.

We can specifically click on certain widgets on the dashboard, such as Total Queries, which will take us to the report, and also provide live feeds of what's coming in.

docs.title: Unbound Checks
docs.text:
On the Dashboard, find the Upstream Servers widget, and check over which upstream servers are appearing:

![[Pasted image 20260815162849.png|397]]

We can see for example, that our Unbound DNS is working, as it is showing with private IP Address 172.21.0.2#53, which is used by the Unbound Docker container (Docker containers usually use 172.x.x.x). Inside the docker container itself, it will be using IP 127.0.0.1.

These next settings should be set automatically by the installation, but good to check anyway. Under Settings > DNS, untick all Upstream DNS Servers, and add on the Unbound custom DNS as so:

In the same area, also set Interface settings to 'Permit all origins'. **Note: As mentioned, this may be set already by the Compose file. If so, this will be greyed out, and you cannot change it. This would only be changeable by amending the Compose file, and re-creating the Docker container.

This setting needs to be set to 'Permit all origins', as this allows both our Pihole and Unbound docker containers to communicate with each other. This is due to them both using separate docker networks, showing as this they're coming from outside the local subnet.

We can lastly run two commands in the console, to check that it is returning our container's 172.x.x.x IP as the DNS Domain:

# Check if Pihole is using Unbound
docker exec -it pihole nslookup example.com unbound

# Test from another device
nslookup example.com 192.168.x.x

Both should return the following:

unbound 

Server: unbound
Address: 172.21.0.3#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name: example.com
Address 104.20.32.154

192.168.x.x 

Server: 192.168.x.x
Address: 192.168.x.x#53

Non-authoritative answer:
Name: example.com
Address: 172.66.147.243

The unbound block will show 172.x.x.x if successful, showing that it is using the docker IP for the unbound container.

The 192.168.x.x will show the same IP if successful, showing that your external device is successfully reaching Pihole.

docs.title: 5. DNS Settings
docs.text:
For domains using Nginx, to redirect to specified IPs + Ports, we need to add each local domain entry to point to the Raspberry Pi IP, where Nginx is hosted.

This is so that once the request is received to connect onto the local domain, it is forwarded straight to Nginx, that then deals with the reverse proxy side.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For example, Proxmox is currently hosted on a different server using IP example 192.168.0.56, and port 8005. The reverse proxy is setup on Nginx, hosted on 192.168.0.123, with code blocks setup in file /etc/nginx/sites-available/your.sites (refer to the Proxmox note under Nginx RP Blocks folder). The IP that proxmox.user.local points to will therefore be 192.168.0.123, as we want to forward it to Nginx to deal with:

![[Pasted image 20260730224916.png]]

docs.title: Simple Local Domain Setup via Pihole
docs.text:
Other domains that do not need to be managed by Nginx, can point directly to their designated IPs. To find the configuration for this, and add new domains, we can follow through these simple steps:

  1. In the Pihole admin portal, navigate to Settings > Local DNS Records
  2. In the Local DNS records pane, within the Domain table, enter the full domain name, alongside it's associated IP
  3. Once entered, click the green + symbol

docs.title: 6. Domain Block Lists
docs.text:
One of the main features of Pihole, is it's ability to block numerous queries and domains on a network level, meaning any device connected to the network it's running on, will have these domains automatically blocked. This is particularly useful for blocking ADs!

With Pihole up and running, we can add a block list via the Web Interface, which is essentially a simple list full of domains we want to block.

docs.title: Obtaining a blocklist URL link
docs.text:
To find a particular block list to add to our Pihole, we can search the web for various lists created by the community. For me, I have used Hagezi's Ultimate blocklist, found on his GitHub page. You can find this on the following URL: https://github.com/hagezi/dns-blocklists

To obtain the blocklist link, scroll down the README, and save the 'Adblock' link (which states it can be used for Pihole) under the intensity level you'd like to choose:

![[Pasted image 20260817214434.png]]

This method will be similar on any other GitHub page, or site you use, by copying the link to the list.

PLEASE NOTE - The blocklist I am currently using, is considered aggressive, and therefore may break certain websites. I therefore tend to manually permit certain domains if I find them to completely break sites that I want to visit, which I will show how to do further down this section.

docs.title: Adding to Pihole
docs.text:
Once you've obtained the link to the blocklist you'd like to add, we can follow the steps below to add this to Pihole:

  1. Login to Pihole, using the login details setup in the installation process.
  2. Navigate to Lists under Group Management
  3. Here, you will see the Add a new subscribed list panel, and the Subscribed lists panel. Currently, your subscribed lists should be empty. This will be where your active lists will sit. To add a new list, we will need to paste the saved blocklist URL we obtained earlier into the Address field, and add a chosen comment: ![[Pasted image 20260817214929.png]]
  4. Press Add blocklist
  5. This will then appear under your Subscribed lists, with status Enabled:

![[Pasted image 20260817215039.png]]

docs.title: Allowing certain domains
docs.text:
As mentioned previously, if you have an aggressive blocklist, that may have broken a particular website you're using, it is handy to be able to allow that particular domain through as an exception. To do this, we first will need to identify which domain is being blocked. We can find this by using the Query Log.

Load or perform the certain action that is not working correctly, e.g. Facebook comments, and look for the domain that is being blocked during that moment. For example, as soon as I attempt to open Facebook comments, I can find the following being blocked:

![[Pasted image 20260817221504.png]]

A quick way to allow these through, is to click on Allow as highlighted in the screenshot above. Once allowed, we can view these in the Domains tab, under Group Management:

![[Pasted image 20260817221613.png]]

On these entries, you can add a comment to note the reason for allowing it, so you can easily keep track. I would then recommend updating the Gravity list, to apply the changes...

docs.title: Updating Gravity List
docs.text:
When you have added a new blocklist, it is always recommended to immediately update the gravity list via Pihole. The gravity list is the main compiled database of blocked domains, where Pihole downloads the addresses from your subscribed lists, combines them, and removes any duplicates that may crop up when you have multiple lists. Once updated, all your lists should be active on Pihole.

To do this, click through the following settings:

  1. In the Pihole interface, click on Tools > Update Gravity
  2. Click Update
  3. You should see the following command portal appear, showing you if the update was successful. Any errors will also appear if it has failed to update all: ![[Pasted image 20260817215712.png]]

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Throughout the guides, many directories, IPs, and usernames will be defaulted to the below list. This is to benefit my privacy. The below are as follows:

  • /home/user

  • x.user.local
    • Your local domain, x being the service

docs.text:
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;

    server_name example.com www.example.com;
    return 301 https://example.com;
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;

proxy_pass - As we are using a docker network, which this service is connected to, we can simply call it's docker container name, followed by it's default port 8000.
